result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.cmty_k_clique()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find overlapping communities by k-clique percolation. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L26875-L26951){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.cmty_k_clique(k=3) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![k-clique communities](/assets/graphs/cmty-k-clique.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Two triangles A, B, C and B, C, D share an edge, so they merge into one community (accent color); triangle D, E, F shares only node D with it and forms a second community (teal). The two tinted regions overlap at D, which belongs to both. The pendant G is in no triangle and in no community." width="100%"} The clique percolation method (Palla et al., 2005) builds communities out of cliques. A *k-clique* is a set of `k` nodes that are all connected to one another. Two k-cliques are adjacent if they share `k - 1` nodes, and a k-clique community is everything that can be reached by "rolling" a k-clique from one adjacent k-clique to the next. Unlike partitioning methods, communities found this way can **overlap**: a node in several tightly knit groups belongs to all of them, which suits social networks where a person has a family, a workplace and a sports team. Nodes in no k-clique (for example, nodes of degree below `k - 1`) belong to no community. Larger `k` gives fewer, smaller, more cohesive communities. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [k]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[3]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : The clique size. Must be at least `2`; with `k=2` the communities are the connected components (minus isolated nodes). Default is `3` (triangles). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The communities, each a sorted list of node IDs, largest first. Communities may share nodes, and not every node needs to appear. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `k` is below `2` or the graph is directed. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Two triangle-rich groups share node D, which belongs to both communities, while the pendant node G belongs to neither: ::: {#ddd5bd74 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("B", "C"), ("B", "D"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("D", "F"), ("E", "F"), ("F", "G")]) ) label = graph.get_label_from_id [[label(n) for n in community] for community in graph.cmty_k_clique(k=3)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [['A', 'B', 'C', 'D'], ['D', 'E', 'F']] ``` ::: :::
